warmup.q: An FX flow emits a cached rate, then calls a provider inside withTimeout(50). Below it sits .catch { emit(fallbackRate) }. The provider takes 100 ms. What does the collector get?
options: The cached rate, then the timeout escapes, because catch never handles a CancellationException
The cached rate, then the fallback rate
Nothing at all: the timeout cancels the collector
The cached rate, and then the flow completes normally with nothing else
warmup.why: withTimeout throws TimeoutCancellationException inside the upstream while the collecting job is still active. To catch that is an upstream failure like any other, so the action runs and emits the fallback. What catch lets pass is the cancellation of the collecting job itself, and exceptions thrown below it.

sections.h: A catch is a net under the upstream, and it checks who threw
sections.html:
An FX rate flow calls a slow provider inside withTimeout(50), and a catch below it emits a fallback rate. The provider takes 100 ms. Most people expect the timeout to fly past the catch, because "catch doesn't handle cancellation" and a timeout is a CancellationException. Run it, then run a second version where the caller's own job is cancelled instead:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: onErrorResume handles what comes from above it; dispose() is a cancel signal
Flux.concat(Flux.just(cachedRate), provider.call().timeout(Duration.ofMillis(50)))
    .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.just(fallbackRate))
    .subscribe(this::show);               // case 2: the subscription is disposed meanwhile
Kotlin
flow { emit(cachedRate); emit(withTimeout(50) { provider.call() }) }   // the call takes 100 ms
    .catch { e -> emit(fallbackRate) }
    .collect { show(it) }                 // case 2: the request scope calls job.cancel() meanwhile

Here is what the Try it prints for five ways the request can end:

How it ends The catch action runs The caller sees
the provider throws IOException yes nothing
the provider throws CancellationException yes nothing
withTimeout fires inside the provider call yes, with TimeoutCancellationException nothing
the collector's ledger write fails no IllegalStateException: ledger write failed
the caller's job is cancelled no JobCancellationException

You know from lesson 2 of this track that an exception thrown by the collector comes back out of emit, up into the upstream's code, and that emitting again after that breaks exception transparency. So when the upstream's collect throws, catch has to work out who threw. Build it by hand and the rule falls out:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: the same bookkeeping around a push-style source and a Consumer
static <T> void myCatch(Consumer<Consumer<T>> upstream, Consumer<T> downstream, Function<Throwable, T> action) {
    RuntimeException[] fromDownstream = {null};
    try {
        upstream.accept(v -> { try { downstream.accept(v); } catch (RuntimeException e) { fromDownstream[0] = e; throw e; } });
    } catch (RuntimeException e) {
        if (e == fromDownstream[0]) throw e;                                   // below the net
        if (Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) throw e;                   // our own task was cancelled
        downstream.accept(action.apply(e));                                    // an upstream failure
    }
}
Kotlin
fun <T> Flow<T>.myCatch(action: suspend FlowCollector<T>.(Throwable) -> Unit): Flow<T> = flow {
    var fromDownstream: Throwable? = null
    try {
        collect { value -> try { emit(value) } catch (e: Throwable) { fromDownstream = e; throw e } }
    } catch (e: Throwable) {
        if (e === fromDownstream) throw e                                              // below the net
        if (e is CancellationException && !currentCoroutineContext().isActive) throw e // our job is cancelled
        action(e)                                                                      // an upstream failure
    }
}

The library's catch does the same bookkeeping. It wraps the downstream emit, remembers what came out of it, and rethrows that. It also rethrows when the exception is the cancellation cause of the collecting job. Everything else goes to your action. Picture a net under the upstream half of the pipe. Anything that falls from above lands in it, including a CancellationException the upstream throws while the job is still active. The job's own cancellation passes through, and whatever the collector drops falls below the net, straight to the caller.

So catch ignores the cancellation of the collector, not every CancellationException. For a provider call that is usually what you want: a timeout becomes a fallback. If not, rethrow CancellationException in the action. And the net only covers what is above it. Move the ledger write into onEach above the catch and call collect() with no lambda, or launchIn(scope). A caught error still ends the upstream: flowOf(1, 2, 3).map { fails on 2 }.catch { emit(-1) } gives 1 and -1, and 3 is never produced.

Check yourself: catch sits above map, and map throws. Who handles it?

steps: Open CatchNet.kt. For each of the five cases, predict whether the net catches it and what the caller sees.
Run it. Each case runs twice: once with the library's catch, once with myCatch from this section. Check that the two lines always agree.
In myCatch, delete the line that rethrows fromDownstream and run again. Which case changes, and what does the caller see now?

code.html: package workbench.flows.l06 import kotlinx.coroutines.CancellationException import kotlinx.coroutines.awaitCancellation import kotlinx.coroutines.currentCoroutineContext import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.FlowCollector import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.catch import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.isActive import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeout import java.io.IOException // catch, built by hand: remember what the downstream threw, and leave our own job's cancellation alone. private fun <T> Flow<T>.myCatch(action: suspend FlowCollector<T>.(Throwable) -> Unit): Flow<T> = flow { var fromDownstream: Throwable? = null try { collect { value -> try { emit(value) } catch (e: Throwable) { fromDownstream = e; throw e } // 1. who threw? } } catch (e: Throwable) { if (e === fromDownstream) throw e // 2. not ours: below the net if (e is CancellationException && !currentCoroutineContext().isActive) throw e // 3. our job is cancelled action(e) // 4. an upstream failure } } private fun describe(e: Throwable?) = e?.let { "${it::class.simpleName}: ${it.message?.lineSequence()?.first()}" } ?: "nothing" // One FX rate request, five ways for it to end. private val cases: List<Pair<String, Flow<Double>>> = listOf( "provider throws IOException" to flow { emit(0.92); throw IOException("provider reset") }, "provider throws CancellationException" to flow { emit(0.92); throw CancellationException("provider gave up") }, "withTimeout inside the provider call" to flow { emit(0.92); withTimeout(50) { delay(100) }; emit(0.93) }, "the collector's ledger write fails" to flow { emit(0.92); emit(0.93) }, "the caller's job is cancelled" to flow { emit(0.92); awaitCancellation() }, ) private fun run(label: String, net: String, f: Flow<Double>) { var caught: Throwable? = null val netted = if (net == "catch") f.catch { caught = it; emit(-1.0) } else f.myCatch { caught = it; emit(-1.0) } val got = mutableListOf<Double>() var callerSaw: Throwable? = null runBlocking { val job = launch { try { netted.collect { got += it; if (label.startsWith("the collector") && it == 0.92) error("ledger write failed") } } catch (e: Throwable) { callerSaw = e; if (e !is CancellationException) Unit else throw e } } if (label.startsWith("the caller")) { delay(10); job.cancel() } job.join() } println(" %-8s got %-12s net caught %-48s caller saw %s".format(net, got, describe(caught), describe(callerSaw))) } fun main() { for ((label, f) in cases) { println("== $label") run(label, "catch", f) run(label, "myCatch", f) } }

rates.doOnNext(CatchNetJava::save) : rates; pipeline = pipeline.onErrorResume(e -> { caught[0] = e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage(); return Mono.just(-1.0); }); if (!saveAboveTheNet) pipeline = pipeline.doOnNext(CatchNetJava::save); String callerSaw = "nothing"; try { pipeline.doOnNext(got::add).blockLast(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { callerSaw = e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage(); } System.out.printf("%-44s got %-12s net caught %-58s caller saw %s%n", label, got, caught[0], callerSaw); } static void save(double rate) { // the ledger write fails on the second rate if (rate == 0.93) throw new IllegalStateException("ledger write failed"); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { run("provider fails with IOException", Flux.concat(Flux.just(0.92), Flux.error(new IOException("provider reset"))), false); run("provider is slow: timeout(50 ms) above the net", Flux.concat(Flux.just(0.92), Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(100)).thenReturn(0.95)).timeout(Duration.ofMillis(50)), false); run("ledger write below the net", Flux.just(0.92, 0.93), false); run("ledger write above the net (doOnNext first)", Flux.just(0.92, 0.93), true); String[] caught = {"nothing"}; Disposable subscription = Flux.concat(Flux.just(0.92), Flux.<Double>never()) .onErrorResume(e -> { caught[0] = e.toString(); return Mono.empty(); }) .doFinally(signal -> System.out.printf("%-44s doFinally %s, net caught %s%n", "the subscriber cancels", signal, caught[0])) .subscribe(); Thread.sleep(20); subscription.dispose(); } }

try.expect: The first three cases get [0.92, -1.0] and the caller sees nothing: the net caught an IOException, a CancellationException and a TimeoutCancellationException ("Timed out waiting for 50 ms"). The ledger failure and the job cancellation pass: the caller sees IllegalStateException: ledger write failed and JobCancellationException. catch and myCatch agree on every line. Without the fromDownstream check, the ledger case runs the action and emits again after the downstream failed, and the flow throws IllegalStateException: Flow exception transparency is violated. In Reactor, the ledger write fails the stream when it sits below onErrorResume and is handled when it sits above it.

sections.h: A retry collects the upstream again, from the top
sections.html:
The acquirer's settlement feed resets after payment-2 on the first attempt, and the import wraps it in retry(3). What does the ledger receive?

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: retry re-subscribes, so a cold Flux replays from the top too
List<String> received = Flux.defer(acquirer::feed).retry(3).collectList().block();
// [payment-1, payment-2, payment-1, payment-2, payment-3]
Kotlin
val received = feed.retry(3).toList()
// [payment-1, payment-2, payment-1, payment-2, payment-3]

Two payments posted twice. retryWhen is a loop around the same bookkeeping as catch. When the upstream fails with an exception that came from above the net, it calls your predicate with the cause and an attempt number. If the predicate says yes, it collects the upstream again, and a cold flow is a recipe: collecting it again runs it again from the top. Values that were already emitted are emitted again. Picture rewinding a tape: everything already played plays again.

The counting follows from the loop. retry(n) is retryWhen { cause, attempt -> attempt < n && predicate(cause) }, so retry(2) on a flow that always fails collects it 3 times, and then the third exception comes out. retry(0) fails when you build the flow with Expected positive amount of retries, but had 0. The default is Long.MAX_VALUE, which retries forever. attempt is 0 on the first failure, and with retry(n, predicate) the predicate is no longer called once the attempts run out.

A backoff is a delay inside the predicate:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: Reactor's backoff spec (jitter off, so the times are exact)
feed.retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)).jitter(0)
        .filter(e -> e instanceof IOException));
Kotlin
feed.retryWhen { cause, attempt ->
    val retry = cause is IOException && attempt < 3
    if (retry) delay(100L shl attempt.toInt())        // 100, 200, 400 ms
    retry
}

Against a call that always fails, both collect at 0, 100, 300 and 700 ms. Then they differ. Flow gives up by letting the original IOException out. Reactor wraps it in a RetryExhaustedException (Retries exhausted: 3/3, the real error as its cause), and in production it adds jitter (0.5 by default, from lesson 5 of the reactive track). Flow has no jitter, no cap and no exhaustion type. You write those yourself, which is what the lab does.

Like catch, a retry never fires for an exception the collector threw or for the caller's own cancellation. It does fire for a TimeoutCancellationException from a timeout() above it, and the last section builds on that.

The replay is the part that hurts in payments. Every consumer after a retry must be idempotent. De-duplicate by payment id (one set per collection), or make the source resumable from a cursor or a Kafka offset, so a retry starts where the last attempt stopped.

Check yourself: retry(3) on a stream that fails after its second element on every attempt. How many times does the collector see element 1?

alt.html: package workbench.flows.l06; import reactor.core.Exceptions; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.util.retry.Retry; import java.io.IOException; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; // Closest Java equivalent: Reactor's retry re-subscribes, so a cold Flux replays from the top too. public class RetryReplayJava { static long t0; static boolean quiet; public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("== a payment feed resets after payment-2 on the first attempt; retry(3)"); AtomicInteger attempt = new AtomicInteger(); Flux<String> feed = Flux.defer(() -> { int n = attempt.incrementAndGet(); return n == 1 ? Flux.concat(Flux.just("payment-1", "payment-2"), Flux.error(new IOException("stream reset"))) : Flux.just("payment-1", "payment-2", "payment-3"); }); System.out.println(" ledger received " + feed.retry(3).collectList().block()); System.out.println("== Retry.backoff(3, 100 ms) with jitter off, on a call that always fails (real time)"); quiet = true; backoff(); // a silent first round loads the classes, so the timings below are clean quiet = false; backoff(); } static void backoff() { AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger(); Flux<String> psp = Flux.defer(() -> { long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; String line = String.format(" call %d at about %d ms", calls.incrementAndGet(), Math.round(ms / 50.0) * 50); if (!quiet) System.out.println(line); return Flux.error(new IOException("PSP timeout")); }); t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { psp.retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)).jitter(0)).blockLast(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { if (!quiet) System.out.println(" caller saw " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage() + "; isRetryExhausted=" + Exceptions.isRetryExhausted(e) + "; cause: " + e.getCause()); } } }

try.expect: The ledger receives [payment-1, payment-2, payment-1, payment-2, payment-3]. retry(2) collects 3 times: [p1, p2, p1, p2, p1, p2, FALLBACK], and retry(0) is rejected with "Expected positive amount of retries, but had 0". The backoff calls come at 0, 100, 300 and 700 ms, then the original IOException reaches the catch. With the predicate, an IOException is not retried, so you get [p1, p2, FALLBACK] after 1 collection. Reactor replays the same five payments, calls at about 0, 100, 300 and 700 ms, and ends with RetryExhaustedException: Retries exhausted: 3/3.

sections.h: The onCompletion bell rings once, and its cause is not always a failure
sections.html:
A metrics hook counts each FX lookup as a success or a failure. Lookups go through first(). In the dashboard, every lookup is a failure:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: doFinally reports a signal type instead of a cause
rates(pair)
    .doFinally(signal -> { if (signal == SignalType.ON_COMPLETE) metrics.ok(); else metrics.failed(signal); })
    .next()
    .block();
Kotlin
rates(pair)
    .onCompletion { cause -> if (cause == null) metrics.ok() else metrics.failed(cause) }
    .first()

onCompletion is a try/finally around the upstream, placed exactly where you wrote it. It runs once, and its cause says what passed through that position on the way out:

How the flow ended cause
completed normally null
the upstream threw IOException: provider reset
the collector threw IllegalStateException: ledger write failed
a map below threw, and a catch below that swallowed it IllegalStateException: map failed
above take(1) or first() AbortFlowException: Flow was aborted, no more elements needed
below take(1) null
the collecting job was cancelled JobCancellationException: StandaloneCoroutine was cancelled

first() stops the upstream the way lesson 2 of this track described: it throws AbortFlowException, a CancellationException, out of the upstream's emit. Everything above it sees that exception go by, so the hook counts a stopped flow as a failed one. Below take(1) the flow just ended, so the cause is null. Picture a bell at the end of the line that rings once with a tag. The tag "aborted, no more needed" is only visible to stations above the take. The fix is to classify in order: null is success, a CancellationException is cancelled or stopped early, anything else is a failure.

onCompletion can emit, but only on success: flowOf("a", "b").onCompletion { if (it == null) emit("Done") } gives a, b, Done. After a failure, emit throws the original cause again. Use catch to emit a replacement.

The terminal operators fail in specific ways, and they stop the upstream at different points. first() on an empty flow throws NoSuchElementException: Expected at least one element. single() throws NoSuchElementException: Flow is empty, or IllegalArgumentException: Flow has more than one element. On a three-element flow, first() pulls 1 element and single() pulls 2 before it fails. Reactor's single() says Source was a (constant) empty and throws IndexOutOfBoundsException: Source emitted more than one item instead.

Check yourself: onCompletion sits below take(1), and the collector throws on the first element. What is cause?

alt.html: package workbench.flows.l06; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import java.io.IOException; // Closest Java equivalent of onCompletion: Reactor's doFinally, which gets a signal type instead of a cause. public class CompletionCausesJava { static void quietly(Runnable r) { try { r.run(); } catch (RuntimeException ignored) { } } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("== doFinally: how did the Flux end?"); Flux.just(1, 2).doFinally(s -> System.out.println(" success: " + s)).blockLast(); quietly(() -> Flux.concat(Flux.just(1), Flux.<Integer>error(new IOException("provider reset"))) .doFinally(s -> System.out.println(" upstream failure: " + s)).blockLast()); Flux.just(1, 2, 3).doFinally(s -> System.out.println(" above take(1): " + s)) .take(1).doFinally(s -> System.out.println(" below take(1): " + s)).blockLast(); System.out.println("== terminal operators"); for (var c : new Object[][] {{"Flux.empty().single()", Flux.empty()}, {"Flux.just(1, 2).single()", Flux.just(1, 2)}}) { try { System.out.printf(" %-28s %s%n", c[0], ((Flux<?>) c[1]).single().block()); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.printf(" %-28s throws %s: %s%n", c[0], e.getClass().getName(), e.getMessage()); } } } }

try.expect: null for success and below take(1). IOException: provider reset for the upstream failure, IllegalStateException: ledger write failed for the collector failure, IllegalStateException: map failed even though a catch below swallowed it. AbortFlowException: Flow was aborted, no more elements needed above take(1) and above first(), and JobCancellationException: StandaloneCoroutine was cancelled for job.cancel(). single() pulls 2 elements and first() pulls 1. Reactor reports onComplete, onError, cancel above take(1) and onComplete below it.

sections.h: A timeout throws a cancellation, and its position sets its meaning
sections.html:
Put it together for a provider that has stopped answering. Each call takes 1,000 ms. The chain gives every call 300 ms, retries with backoff and then falls back. When does the fallback answer?

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: the Reactor chain from lesson 5 of the reactive track
primary.rate(pair)
    .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(300))
    .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)).jitter(0).filter(this::isTransient))
    .onErrorResume(e -> Exceptions.isRetryExhausted(e) || isTransient(e), e -> fallback.rate(pair));
Kotlin
primary.rate(pair)
    .timeout(300.milliseconds)            // per attempt; @FlowPreview
    .retryWithBackoff()                   // 3 retries: 100, 200, 400 ms
    .catch { e -> if (!isTransient(e)) throw e; emitAll(fallback.rate(pair)) }

The calls start at 0, 400, 900 and 1,600 ms, and each one is cut at +300. At 1,900 ms the primary gives up with Timed out waiting for 300ms, and the fallback answers at 1,930. Reactor's chain prints the same times in real time.

timeout(d) arrived in 1.7.0 and is still @FlowPreview in 1.11.0. It takes a Duration only. It runs the upstream in a producer coroutine and arms a timer only while it waits for the next upstream value. Time the downstream spends on a value doesn't count, but the wait for the first value does. Picture a watchdog egg timer, wound each time the operator starts waiting, paused while the collector is busy. When it rings it throws TimeoutCancellationException, and that is a CancellationException.

That one fact explains the rest of the chain. The timeout comes from above retryWhen while the job is active, so retryWhen can retry it, but only if isTransient lists TimeoutCancellationException, because a timeout is not an IOException. Position sets the meaning: above retryWhen it limits each attempt, below it limits the whole sequence, waits included. Add .timeout(1.seconds) after the retries and the same provider gets calls at 0, 400 and 900, the budget fires at 1,000, and the fallback answers at 1,030. The catch at the end filters on isTransient, so a bad pair (IllegalArgumentException) reaches the caller at 20 ms with no retry and no fallback. And when the fallback fails too, the caller sees the fallback's error. The primary's error is not attached.

The cancellation nature bites when the flow runs in the background. Uncaught inside launch or launchIn, a timeout just ends that coroutine as cancelled. No CoroutineExceptionHandler runs, and the parent scope keeps going, because handlers ignore CancellationException. Your FX refresher stops and nobody hears it. Translate it at the edge: .catch { e -> if (e is TimeoutCancellationException) throw ProviderTimeout(e) else throw e }, and the handler gets ProviderTimeout with the timeout as its cause. Reactor's timeout signals java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException, which is an ordinary error, so the trap doesn't exist there.

Two notes for tests. Under runTest, withTimeout has a different message ("Timed out after 50ms of virtual (kotlinx.coroutines.test) time..."), so assert on the exception type, never the text. And TimeoutCancellationException has no public constructor, so produce one with a real timeout() under virtual time, as the lab does.

Check yourself: where does .timeout(1.seconds) go to be a per-attempt limit instead of a budget?

steps: Open FlakyProvider.kt. Before you run it, write down when each of cases A to E ends, and how many calls each provider gets.
Run it on virtual time and compare. Case E is case B with an overall timeout(1.seconds) after the retries.

Run FlakyProviderJava, the Reactor version of case B, in real time.

code.html: @file:OptIn(FlowPreview::class) package workbench.flows.l06 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineExceptionHandler import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.FlowPreview import kotlinx.coroutines.Job import kotlinx.coroutines.TimeoutCancellationException import kotlinx.coroutines.currentCoroutineContext import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.catch import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.emitAll import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.launchIn import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.retryWhen import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.single import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.timeout import kotlinx.coroutines.isActive import kotlinx.coroutines.test.StandardTestDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.test.TestCoroutineScheduler import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest import java.io.IOException import kotlin.time.Duration import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.milliseconds import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds @OptIn(kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) private suspend fun now() = currentCoroutineContext()[TestCoroutineScheduler]!!.currentTime private suspend fun log(msg: String) = println("%5d ms %s".format(now(), msg)) /** script(n) says what call n does: a latency in ms, or an exception thrown after 20 ms. */ private class Provider(val name: String, val script: (Int) -> Any) { var calls = 0 fun rate(pair: String): Flow<String> = flow { val n = ++calls log(" $name call $n starts") when (val step = script(n)) { is Long -> { delay(step); emit("$pair 0.92 from $name") } is Throwable -> { delay(20); throw step } } } } private fun transient(e: Throwable) = e is IOException || e is TimeoutCancellationException private fun <T> Flow<T>.backoff(max: Long = 3, first: Duration = 100.milliseconds): Flow<T> = retryWhen { cause, attempt -> if (attempt >= max || !transient(cause)) return@retryWhen false val wait = first * (1L shl attempt.toInt()).toDouble() log(" retry ${attempt + 1} after ${cause::class.simpleName}, waiting $wait") delay(wait) true } private fun case(title: String, primary: Provider, fallback: Provider, budget: Duration? = null) = runTest { println("== $title") var f = primary.rate("USD/EUR").timeout(300.milliseconds).backoff() if (budget != null) f = f.timeout(budget) val rate = f.catch { e -> if (!transient(e)) throw e log(" primary gave up (${e::class.simpleName}: ${e.message}); using the fallback") emitAll(fallback.rate("USD/EUR")) } val outcome = runCatching { rate.single() }.fold({ "result: $it" }, { "caller saw ${it::class.simpleName}: ${it.message}" }) log(" $outcome (primary calls ${primary.calls}, fallback calls ${fallback.calls})") } class ProviderTimeout(cause: Throwable) : Exception("FX provider timed out", cause) fun main() { case("A: two resets, then a 50 ms answer", Provider("primary") { n -> if (n <= 2) IOException("reset") else 50L }, Provider("fallback") { 30L }) case("B: the primary always takes 1000 ms", Provider("primary") { 1_000L }, Provider("fallback") { 30L }) case("C: a bad pair is not transient", Provider("primary") { IllegalArgumentException("unsupported pair") }, Provider("fallback") { 30L }) case("D: both providers down", Provider("primary") { IOException("primary down") }, Provider("fallback") { IOException("fallback down") }) case("E: B again, with timeout(1s) as an overall budget", Provider("primary") { 1_000L }, Provider("fallback") { 30L }, budget = 1.seconds) println("== a timeout that escapes launchIn is a cancellation: nobody hears it") runTest { val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> println(" handler got ${e::class.simpleName}: ${e.message}") } val scope = CoroutineScope(Job() + handler + StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) val silent = flow { delay(200); emit(1) }.timeout(50.milliseconds).launchIn(scope) silent.join() println(" silent: job cancelled=${silent.isCancelled}, scope active=${scope.isActive}") val loud = flow { delay(200); emit(1) }.timeout(50.milliseconds) .catch { e -> if (e is TimeoutCancellationException) throw ProviderTimeout(e) else throw e } .launchIn(scope) loud.join() println(" loud: job cancelled=${loud.isCancelled}, scope active=${scope.isActive}") } }

alt.title: FlakyProviderJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.flows.l06; import reactor.core.Exceptions; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import reactor.util.retry.Retry; import java.io.IOException; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; // Closest Java equivalent of the flaky-provider pattern: Reactor's timeout, retryWhen(Retry.backoff) and // onErrorResume. Case B: the primary always takes 1000 ms. Real time, so expect a few ms of drift. public class FlakyProviderJava { static long t0; static boolean quiet; static final AtomicInteger primaryCalls = new AtomicInteger(); static void log(String msg) { long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; String line = String.format("%5d ms (about %4d) %s", ms, Math.round(ms / 50.0) * 50, msg); if (!quiet) System.out.println(line); } static Mono<String> primary() { return Mono.defer(() -> { log(" primary call " + primaryCalls.incrementAndGet() + " starts"); return Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(1_000)).thenReturn("USD/EUR 0.92 from primary"); }); } static Mono<String> fallback() { return Mono.defer(() -> { log(" fallback call starts"); return Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(30)).thenReturn("USD/EUR 0.92 from fallback"); }); } static boolean transientError(Throwable e) { return e instanceof IOException || e instanceof TimeoutException; } public static void main(String[] args) { quiet = true; run(); // a silent first round loads the classes, so the timings below are clean quiet = false; run(); } static void run() { primaryCalls.set(0); t0 = System.nanoTime(); String rate = primary() .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(300)) // per attempt .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)).jitter(0).filter(FlakyProviderJava::transientError)) .onErrorResume(e -> Exceptions.isRetryExhausted(e) || transientError(e), e -> { log(" primary gave up: " + e.getMessage() + " (cause: " + e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName() + ")"); return fallback(); }) .block(); log(" result: " + rate + " (primary calls " + primaryCalls.get() + ")"); } }

try.expect: A ends at 390 ms from the primary (3 calls). B: calls at 0, 400, 900 and 1,600, the primary gives up at 1,900 with "Timed out waiting for 300ms", and the fallback answers at 1,930. C: the caller sees IllegalArgumentException at 20 ms, with no retry. D: the caller sees IOException: fallback down at 800. E: the budget fires at 1,000 ("Timed out waiting for 1s") and the fallback answers at 1,030. In the launchIn block the silent version leaves the scope active and calls no handler; the loud version reaches the handler and the scope is no longer active. Reactor's case B starts calls at about 0, 400, 900 and 1,600 ms and answers from the fallback at about 1,950.

analogy: A water pipe from a reservoir (the upstream) to a tap (the collector), with a net stretched across it. Debris that falls from the reservoir side lands in the net, and catch can replace it with clean water. A rock dropped at the tap end was never above the net, so it goes straight to whoever holds the tap. When the city shuts the main (your job is cancelled), the shut-off goes past the net on purpose. retry is draining the pipe and refilling it from the reservoir, so the water you already drank comes through again. onCompletion is a bell at one point on the pipe that rings once when the flow stops there, with a tag saying why. The analogy breaks at timeouts: in a real pipe an alarm is not the same as a shut-off, but in Flow a timeout is a kind of cancellation, which is why it slips silently out of a launch unless you translate it.
world: Your Quarkus service quotes card payments in the customer's currency, and the FX provider has a bad week. Wrap the call as in the last section: timeout(300.milliseconds) per attempt, retryWithBackoff() for IOException and TimeoutCancellationException, an overall budget that fits the checkout's own deadline, then a fallback to the second provider. The request's coroutine is cancelled when the client disconnects, and because catch and retryWhen skip the job's own cancellation, no retry or fallback call is wasted on a user who has left. The settlement import is the other side of the same coin. If it reads a Kafka topic or a paged acquirer API through a retried flow, a retry replays records you already posted. Make the ledger write idempotent on the payment id, or resume from the last committed offset, before you add the retry.
mistake: Putting retry on a stream that has side effects and assuming it continues where it failed. A retry collects the upstream again from the top, so every payment before the failure is delivered again: [payment-1, payment-2, payment-1, payment-2, payment-3]. People make this mistake because retries are usually shown on single calls, where replaying is exactly what you want. The fix is to make the consumer idempotent (de-duplicate by payment id, one set per collection, or let the database reject a second insert of the same key) or to make the source resumable, so the retry starts from a cursor or Kafka offset. A close second: onCompletion { if (cause != null) metrics.failed() } above first() or take, which counts every early stop as a failure because the cause there is an AbortFlowException.

compare.title: One flaky provider call, as a Reactor chain and as a Flow chain

java.title: Reactor
java.html: Mono<Rate> fxRate(String pair) { return Mono.defer(() -> primary.rate(pair)) .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(300)) // TimeoutException: an ordinary error .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)) // jitter 0.5 by default .filter(e -> e instanceof IOException || e instanceof TimeoutException)) .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) // overall budget .onErrorResume(e -> Exceptions.isRetryExhausted(e) || e instanceof TimeoutException, e -> fallback.rate(pair)); // exhausted: RetryExhaustedException }

kotlin.title: Kotlin Flow
kotlin.html: @OptIn(FlowPreview::class) fun fxRate(pair: String): Flow<Rate> = primary.rate(pair) .timeout(300.milliseconds) // TimeoutCancellationException: a cancellation .retryWhen { cause, attempt -> // no jitter, no cap unless you write them val retry = isTransient(cause) && attempt < 3 if (retry) delay(100L shl attempt.toInt()) retry } .timeout(1.seconds) // overall budget .catch { e -> if (!isTransient(e)) throw e; emitAll(fallback.rate(pair)) } // the original error

compare.note: The two chains have the same shape and, with jitter off, the same timeline. What differs is what the errors are. Reactor's timeout signals TimeoutException, an ordinary error, while Flow's throws TimeoutCancellationException, a CancellationException, so you must list it in isTransient, and a timeout that escapes a launch ends that coroutine silently. Reactor wraps exhausted retries in RetryExhaustedException, while retryWhen lets the original exception out. Reactor's backoff has jitter, a cap and an exhaustion error built in, and in Flow you write the policy yourself. One thing Flow gives you for free: catch and retryWhen never act on the collecting job's own cancellation, so a caller that goes away stops the whole chain without a retry or a fallback call.

worked.title: Wrap the FX provider call, one decision at a time

lab.title: A flaky FX provider: timeouts, backoff, a fallback, and a feed that replays
steps: Run the tests once. All 12 fail. Every timing in ErrorsTest is virtual, and each test name states the rule.
In Retries.kt, write isTransient, then retryWithBackoff with retryWhen. The wait before retry k is first * 2^k, capped at max.

In FxRates.kt, write fxRate: timeout(300.milliseconds), then retryWithBackoff(), then a catch that rethrows non-transient errors and otherwise emits all of the fallback's flow. Predict the four provider tests' times before you run them.
Read the cancellation test. Work out why your fxRate passes it without any extra code.
Fix uniquePayments so a retry can't deliver a payment twice, and so a second collection still delivers everything.
hints: retryWhen's lambda gets (cause, attempt), and attempt starts at 0. Return false to let the original exception out, and delay before returning true.
Duration times Double works: first * (1L shl attempt.toInt()).toDouble(), then minOf(..., max).
timeout is @FlowPreview in 1.11.0, so fxRate needs @OptIn(FlowPreview::class). Without it you only get a warning.
For uniquePayments, create the set of seen ids inside a flow { } builder, so each collection gets a fresh one. A set created outside it is shared by every collector.

drill.title: Write catch from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write fun <T> Flow<T>.myCatch(action: suspend FlowCollector<T>.(Throwable) -> Unit): Flow<T> with flow { }. It must rethrow what the downstream threw, rethrow the cancellation of its own job, and hand everything else to action. Then say which of these reaches action: an upstream withTimeout firing, the collector throwing, job.cancel().

answer.html: fun <T> Flow<T>.myCatch(action: suspend FlowCollector<T>.(Throwable) -> Unit): Flow<T> = flow { var fromDownstream: Throwable? = null try { collect { value -> try { emit(value) } catch (e: Throwable) { fromDownstream = e; throw e } // 1. remember what the collector threw } } catch (e: Throwable) { if (e === fromDownstream) throw e // 2. below the net if (e is CancellationException && !currentCoroutineContext().isActive) throw e // 3. our job action(e) // 4. from upstream } } // Only the upstream withTimeout reaches action: it is a CancellationException, but our job is still active.

alt.html: // Closest Java equivalent: a push-style source and a Consumer, with the same three checks static <T> void myCatch(Consumer<Consumer<T>> upstream, Consumer<T> downstream, Function<Throwable, T> action) { RuntimeException[] fromDownstream = {null}; try { upstream.accept(v -> { try { downstream.accept(v); } catch (RuntimeException e) { fromDownstream[0] = e; throw e; } // 1. remember what the consumer threw }); } catch (RuntimeException e) { if (e == fromDownstream[0]) throw e; // 2. below the net if (Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) throw e; // 3. our own task was cancelled downstream.accept(action.apply(e)); // 4. from upstream } }

recap: A downstream exception comes out of emit. catch remembers it and rethrows it, and it rethrows its own job's cancellation. Everything else from upstream reaches the action, a CancellationException or TimeoutCancellationException included.
Work in collect { } is below the net. Put it in onEach above catch, then call collect() or launchIn.
retry(n) means n retries, n + 1 collections, and each one replays the upstream from the top. Consumers after a retry must be idempotent.
retryWhen's attempt starts at 0, a delay in it is the backoff, and the original exception comes out at the end. There is no jitter or exhaustion type unless you write it.
onCompletion's cause is null on success, the exception on failure, JobCancellationException on cancel, and AbortFlowException above take or first.
timeout() throws TimeoutCancellationException, a cancellation. Above retryWhen it limits each attempt, below it is a budget, and uncaught in a launch it ends silently, so translate it.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why catch { emit(fallbackRate) } turns a provider timeout into a fallback, but does nothing when the customer closes the page and the request is cancelled. They thought catch never sees CancellationException. Explain it with the net picture, and say what you'd add if the flow ran in a background launchIn job.
explain.answer: catch is a net under the upstream. It wraps the downstream's emit and remembers anything the collector throws, which it rethrows, and it rethrows the cancellation of its own collecting job. Everything else that falls from above lands in the net. A withTimeout or timeout() inside the provider call throws TimeoutCancellationException while our job is still active, so to catch it's just an upstream failure and the action emits the fallback. When the customer closes the page, the request's job is cancelled. That cancellation is the job's own, so the net lets it pass and no fallback call is made, which is what we want. In a background launchIn job I'd add a translation: if both providers time out, the TimeoutCancellationException would escape the launch as a plain cancellation, no exception handler would run and the refresher would stop silently. So I'd convert it in a catch into a domain ProviderTimeout exception, which the scope's handler logs.

deeper.html:
When both sides fail, the upstream wins. If the collector throws IllegalStateException("collector failed") and the builder's finally then throws IOException("close() failed"), the caller sees the IOException, with the collector's exception in suppressed, and a catch above does not run its action. The Flow KDoc calls this "a semantic equivalent of throwing from finally block", and notes that the exception-handling operators still treat the downstream exception as the root cause.

A failed fallback forgets the primary. flow { throw IOException("primary down") }.catch { emitAll(flow { throw IOException("fallback down") }) } gives the caller IOException: fallback down with no cause and nothing suppressed. If you want both in the logs, attach the primary yourself with addSuppressed before you emit the fallback.

Don't retry from inside catch with emitAll(sameFlow). The catch KDoc points to retryWhen, which retries "without introducing ever-growing stack of suspending calls".

withTimeoutOrNull(250) { flow.toList() } returns null and loses the values that arrived before the deadline. Collect into a list you own (collect { partial += it }) if you need them. Inside runBlocking with a CoroutineName("settlement-import"), the withTimeout message names the coroutine: Coroutine "settlement-import" timed out waiting for 50 ms.

The exact boundary of timeout(100.milliseconds) depends on how the scheduler orders events at the same instant: under virtual time a 100 ms gap did not time out and a 101 ms gap did. Don't build logic on the equality case.

onEmpty { emit(default) } is the counterpart for a flow that completes without a value: a merchant with no fee schedule gets the default fee, and a merchant with one gets theirs.

sources.title: operators/Errors.kt at tag 1.11.0 (catch, retry and retryWhen)
